title: Astronomers find 'intricate structure' in unique object in our galaxy
excerpt: New images show stunning features of the only known supernova remnant of its kind in our galaxy
content:
Scientists have captured in astonishing detail the “intricate structure” of a unique object in our galaxy.

Pa 30 is the only known supernova remnant of its kind in the Milky Way, and is made up of the leftovers from the fatal explosion of a star that was observed almost 850 years ago. Now, using the latest telescopes, astronomers have captured it in precise detail.

It shows the intricate structure of the explosion: something like a fireworks display, as strands reach out into the universe. Those strands are each wide enough to fit the solar system multiple times over.

At its middle sits the “zombie star”, the surviving pieces of the exploded star, unusually sitting right at the centre of the display. That star was seen exploding in 1181 – as recorded separately in Japanese, Chinese and Arabic sources of the time – and the remnant was first spotted by a citizen scientist in 2013.

In the new research, however, astronomers were able to use the Gemini North telescope to reveal a detailed view of that explosion. It showed that what appears at first glance to be streaks akin to a firework are actually long chains of knots, something like pearls on a string.

The explosion sits about 7,500 light years away from Earth. It is the only known object of its kind in the Milky Way – and, though other examples have been seen in other galaxies, its relative proximity means that we can see the leftovers from the explosion at its core.

That is left behind because the supernova was a “Type Iax”, where the explosion does not fully destroy the star itself. Researchers believe it happened after the collision of two white dwarfs – the dense, Earth-sized objects that stars collapse into as they die.

“We can see this much detail because of Pa 30’s proximity to Earth,” said Ilaria Caiazzo, from the Institute of Science and Technology Austria, who helped lead the work. “This proximity makes Pa 30 uniquely valuable for study.”

Though Pa 30 is the only known example of its kind, it might not be alone in our galaxy. There may be others out there waiting to be found, scientists say.

“Reliable historical records of stellar explosions extend back only about a thousand years. For all we know, there might well be similar remnants still lurking in the dark in our own galaxy,” said Tim Cunningham, from the University of Warwick, who also co-led the work. “Today, we are lucky to study an intriguing object we know was observed by astronomers who made three independent historical records of the event centuries before the invention of the telescope.”

The work is reported in a new paper, ‘Detection of knots in the supernova type Iax remnant Pa 30’, in The Astrophysical Journal.
